courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Axioms of Mechanics - Motion of a Body in a Resisting Medium - Motion in a Vertical Circle - Vertical and Circular Motion - Vectors - Composition and Resolution of Forces - Equilibrium of a Particle in a Plane and in Space - Pappus-Guldinus Theorems - Rigid Body - Differentiation of Vectors: Velocity and Acceleration - Harmonic Motion - Circular Motion - Momentum - Energy - Power
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Acquire fundamental concepts in the field of dynamics. • Understand particle motion in one and two dimensions, including velocity, acceleration, distance, and time. • Study vectors, force, Newton's Laws, and the concepts of different frames of reference.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts of mechanics' axioms and types of motion (such as motion in a resisting medium, motion in a vertical circle, and harmonic motion). • Explains the principles of vectors, the composition and resolution of forces, and Newton's Laws of Motion. • Describes the concepts of particle equilibrium in a plane and in space, Pappus-Guldinus theorems, the rigid body, and the concepts related to momentum, energy, and power. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes problems related to the motion of bodies under various conditions (such as motion in a resisting medium or a circle). • Infers how to apply Newton's Laws and the fundamental principles of mechanics to solve complex problems. • Applies concepts of vector differentiation to determine velocity and acceleration in diverse kinematic contexts. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses vectors to compose and resolve forces and to find the equilibrium of a particle in different dimensions. • Executes calculations related to momentum, energy, and power for moving bodies. • Develops problem-solving skills related to harmonic and circular motion. General and Transferable Skills • Collaborates effectively in teams to solve complex problems. • Communicates clearly and effectively about concepts, both in writing and orally. • Thinks critically and systematically when addressing challenges

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: vector algebra, types of forces, moments, couples, equivalence of force systems, equilibrium of bodies in 2D and 3D, equilibrium of structures, and internal forces in beams (shear forces and bending moments). It also covers trusses, equilibrium of heavy cables and distributed loads, and center of gravity (for wires, areas, and volumes). Further topics include moment of inertia and products of inertia, the parallel axis theorem, rotation of axes and principal moments of inertia, virtual work and stability of equilibrium, and an introduction to fluid statics.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: Identify the basic concepts of statics. Become familiar with developments related to statics
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define fundamental concepts in statics, such as types of forces, moments, couples, and center of gravity. • Explain the principles of equilibrium for bodies in 2D and 3D, as well as the equilibrium of various structures. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the equivalence of force systems and internal forces (shear forces and bending moments) in beams and trusses. • Interpret the concepts of moment of inertia, products of inertia, and the parallel axis theorem within the context of statics. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply equilibrium laws to calculate unknown forces in bodies, structures, and heavy cables. • Calculate the center of gravity for different geometric shapes (wires, areas, volumes) and moments of inertia. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve problems. Participate actively in discussions

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: vectors in the plane, the straight line, conic sections, parametric equations of curves in the plane (cycloid, and conic sections), the general second-degree equation in two variables, vectors in space, the distance from a point to a plane, surfaces of revolution, the equation of a straight line, and the plane.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Understand coordinate concepts • Formulate equations of lines and planes • Simplify second-degree equations • Identify second-degree surfaces
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Describe vectors in the plane • Determine the distance from a point to a surface of revolution B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to: • Classify parametric equations of plane curves • Analyze second-degree surfaces C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to: • Solve the general second-degree equation in two variables • Simplify second-degree equations D) Transferable Skills: Students are expected to be able to: • Use information technology tools • Find innovative solutions

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content covers two main areas: Properties of Matter and Heat. Under Properties of Matter, topics include dimensional analysis and its applications, elasticity and its coefficients, surface tension and capillarity, hydrodynamics, fluid motion including Bernoulli's equation and its practical applications, viscosity, diffusion, and osmotic pressure. The Heat section begins with an introduction to the concepts of heat, temperature, and thermal equilibrium, followed by the mechanical equivalent of heat, thermometers, and temperature scales. It also delves into the effect of heat on materials, covering phase transformations, thermal expansion and its applications, the anomalous behavior of water, thermal stresses, and discoloration. Finally, it explores the mechanisms of heat transfer, specifically thermal insulation of buildings and thermal conduction.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Identify the states of matter and their types. • Connect various physical phenomena to the properties of materials. • Understand the effect of heat on materials and the mechanics of heat transfer.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines fundamental concepts related to properties of matter, such as dimensional analysis, elasticity, surface tension, and viscosity. • Explains the principles of fluid motion and Bernoulli's equation, as well as the concepts of diffusion and osmotic pressure. • Describes the concepts of heat, temperature, and thermal equilibrium, along with the effect of heat on materials and phase transformations. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes various physical phenomena and connects them to the properties of materials, such as thermal expansion and the anomalous behavior of water. • Infers how to apply hydrodynamic concepts in diverse practical contexts. • Applies laws and principles of heat transfer (thermal conduction) to understand thermal insulation. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses principles of dimensional analysis to solve physical problems related to material properties. • Executes calculations related to surface tension, viscosity, and elastic coefficients. • Develops a practical understanding of the effects of thermal stresses and discoloration in materials. General and Transferable Skills • Collaborates effectively in analyzing and interpreting complex physical phenomena. • Communicates clearly and effectively about physical concepts related to properties of matter and heat, both in writing and orally. • Thinks critically and systematically when facing new physical challenges and their applications.

courses.courseDescription: This course includes the following topics: Introduction to mathematical logic, sets, Cartesian product, relations and mappings, algebraic systems and binary operations, definitions of group, ring, and field, residue classes, partial fractions, mathematical induction, summation of finite series, convergence and divergence of infinite series, binomial theorem expansions, higher-order determinants, solving systems of linear equations, matrix algebra, and complex number algebra
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to understand fundamental algebraic concepts and theories for analyzing and interpreting practical data, comprehend different algebraic patterns, and draw conclusions related to real-world contexts
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: Upon completing this course, each student is expected to be able to:Understand basic algebraic theories, Define mathematical logic, Identify methods in matrix algebra. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Analyze data, Interpret information, Apply algebraic reasoning. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Solve linear equations, Apply mathematical induction. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to: Think critically, Use a variety of approaches and methods to achieve the best possible outcomes.

courses.courseDescription: This course covers: an introduction to computers, computer components, operating systems, an introduction to computer networks and the internet, computer viruses, utilization of computers in various sectors of society, practical applications using Windows OS, Microsoft Word (word processor), Microsoft Excel (spreadsheets), Microsoft Access (database), Microsoft PowerPoint (presentations), Internet Explorer (web browser), and antivirus software.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will have developed basic concepts and skills in using computers, common operating systems, and related applications, as well as essential internet applications.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: Upon completing this course, students are expected to be able to: Identify the components of a computer, Understand antivirus software, Describe the parts of a computer, Summarize internet applications. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to: Process text documents, Analyze computer operating systems. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to: Design presentations, Apply computer use in various fields, Use spreadsheet software. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to: Use modern technology in daily life , Collaborate effectively with peers.

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Philosophy and Nature of Mathematics - The Interrelation between Philosophy and Mathematics - Mathematics in Babylonian and Ancient Egyptian Civilizations - Contributions of Indians and Chinese - Mathematics among the Greeks - Development of Mathematics in Arabic and Islamic Civilizations - Mathematics and the European Renaissance - Invention of Analytical Geometry and Calculus in the 17th and 18th Centuries - Mathematics in the 19th Century - Non-Euclidean Geometry - Set Theory and Abstract Algebra - Characteristics of Mathematics in the 20th Century.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Understand the philosophical assumptions of mathematics. • Describe the historical developments of mathematics among the Greeks and Muslims. • Identify the role of Europeans in the development of mathematics in recent centuries.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts of the philosophy of mathematics and its nature, as well as the interrelation between philosophy and mathematics. • Explains the historical developments of mathematics in various civilizations, such as Babylonian, Ancient Egyptian, Indian, Chinese, and Greek. • Describes the role of Arabic and Islamic civilizations in the development of mathematics, the invention of analytical geometry and calculus in the 17th and 18th centuries, and the evolution of mathematics in the 19th and 20th centuries (non-Euclidean geometry, set theory, and abstract algebra). Intellectual Skills • Analyzes the characteristics and features of mathematics across different eras and their impact on human intellectual development. • Infers the logical connections and mutual influences between philosophy and mathematical advancements throughout history. • Applies historical concepts to understand the current context of modern mathematical theories. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses the historical method in research and analysis to comprehend the origins of mathematical theories and concepts. • Executes presentations or short research papers on prominent mathematical figures or significant historical periods in mathematics. • Develops critical thinking skills in evaluating mathematical contributions across the ages. General and Transferable Skills • Communicates effectively about statistical results. • Presents interpretations and conclusions clearly and in an organized manner. • Works efficiently within a team to solve problems. • Participates effectively in discussions

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: the concept of a group, types of groups (subgroups, cyclic groups), Lagrange's Theorem, normal subgroups, quotient groups, group homomorphisms, isomorphism theorems, automorphisms of groups, simple groups, Cayley's Theorem and its generalization, symmetry groups, group action on a set, Cauchy's Theorem, Sylow's Theorems and their applications, direct products, and classification of small order groups up to isomorphism
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify the basic concepts of Group Theory. • Understand the applications of Group Theory.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Identify the concept of a group and its various types, such as subgroups and cyclic groups. • Explain fundamental theorems in group theory, such as Lagrange's Theorem and isomorphism theorems. Cognitive Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Analyze the structure of normal subgroups and quotient groups. • Differentiate between simple groups and the classification of groups of small orders. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Apply theorems from group theory, such as Cauchy's and Sylow's Theorems, to solve problems. • Utilize the concept of group action on a set to understand its properties. General Transferable Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about complex ideas in computational processes. • Collaborate effectively with peers in solving mathematical problems.

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Indefinite Integral - Properties of Integration - Integration of Trigonometric Functions - Integration of Inverse Trigonometric Functions - Integration of Exponential Functions - Integration of Logarithmic Functions - Integration of Hyperbolic Functions - Integration of Inverse Hyperbolic Functions - Integration by Partial Fractions - Integration by Parts - Integration by Substitution - Substitution using Algebraic Functions - Substitution using Trigonometric Functions - Integration by Reduction - Deriving General Formulas for the Reduction of: Trigonometric Functions and Hyperbolic Functions - Properties of the Definite Integral - Improper Integral - Using Definite Integral to Find Area - Volumes of Revolution - Finding the Volume of a Sphere - Surface Areas of Revolution - Surface Area of a Sphere.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Understand the properties of integration, the integration of logarithmic and hyperbolic functions, integration by reduction, and definite integrals. • Apply definite integral concepts to calculate areas, volumes, and surface areas of various geometric shapes, including finding the volume and surface area of a sphere. • Acquire knowledge about integration properties, the integration of trigonometric functions, inverse trigonometric functions, exponential functions, and logarithmic functions.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts of indefinite integrals, properties of integration, and the integration of trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic, hyperbolic, and inverse hyperbolic functions. • Explains various integration techniques such as integration by partial fractions, by parts, and by substitution (including algebraic and trigonometric substitutions). • Describes the properties of definite and improper integrals, and how to use definite integrals to find areas, volumes of revolution, and surface areas of revolution. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes complex integration problems and selects the most appropriate method for their solution. • Infers general formulas for the reduction of trigonometric and hyperbolic functions to simplify their integration. • Applies definite integral concepts to calculate areas, volumes, and surface areas of various geometric shapes, including finding the volume and surface area of a sphere. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses different integration techniques skillfully to solve a wide range of functions. • Executes the necessary calculations to find definite and improper integrals accurately. • Develops strategies for solving problems that require combining multiple integration methods. General and Transferable Skills • Collaborates effectively in solving challenging integration problems and discussing solutions. • Communicates clearly and effectively about mathematical concepts and methods related to integration, both in writing and orally. • Thinks critically and systematically when encountering new challenges in calculus.

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: fundamental properties of the real number line, the completeness axiom, countable sets, the Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem, and Cauchy's application. It also covers the basic properties of the topology of real numbers, a study of limits of functions, proving facts about limits, as well as continuity and uniform continuity and the differences between them. The course defines the Riemann integral, Darboux's Theorem and Riemann sums, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, sequences and series of functions, pointwise convergence, and uniform convergence
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify the fundamental properties of the real number field, function limits, and continuity. • Grasp sequences and series. • Recognize the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental properties of the real number line, the completeness axiom, and countable sets. • Explains the concepts of limits of functions, continuity, and uniform continuity, and their distinctions. • Identifies the definition of the Riemann integral, Darboux's Theorem, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes the properties of the topology of real numbers and their implications for function behavior. • Interprets the characteristics of sequences and series of functions, including pointwise and uniform convergence. • Differentiates between various theoretical concepts like the Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem and Cauchy's application. Professional and Practical Skills • Applies the definition of the Riemann integral to evaluate definite integrals. • Uses the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to solve problems involving differentiation and integration. • Calculates pointwise and uniform convergence for given sequences and series of functions. Transferable Skills • Presents interpretations and conclusions clearly and systematically. • Works efficiently as part of a team to solve problems. • Participates actively in discussions

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: coordinate systems (Cartesian and polar coordinates), various forms of equations for a straight line in the plane, the equation of a tangent to a curve in the plane, pairs of straight lines, various forms of the equation of a circle, conic sections (their physical and geometric properties, and methods of drawing them), the polar form of conic sections, and equations of tangents to conic sections.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Understand coordinate systems • Identify different forms of straight-line and circle equations • Analyze and graph conic sections
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify the various forms of straight-line equations in the plane • Explain coordinate systems B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to: • Classify different coordinate systems • Analyze the different forms of the circle equation C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to: • Solve tangent equations for conic sections • Apply different coordinate systems in practical problems D) Transferable Skills: Students are expected to be able to: • Evaluate information effectively • Organize time and prioritize tasks

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: an introduction to numerical analysis, error estimation, solving non-linear equations, interpolation, theories for validating results, numerical integration and differentiation, solving systems of linear equations, matrix analysis methods, an introduction to solving ordinary differential equations, and Gaussian quadratures
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Recognize the importance of using numerical methods to solve various scientific problems. • Explain interpolation methods, numerical integration and differentiation, and matrix analysis methods. • Identify the fundamental principles for solving systems of linear equations and ordinary differential equations. • Apply numerical methods to solve diverse scientific problems, finding approximate solutions to presented issues.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define fundamental concepts in numerical analysis, such as error estimation and solving non-linear equations. • Explain methods of interpolation, numerical integration and differentiation, and matrix analysis methods. • Identify the basic principles for solving systems of linear equations and ordinary differential equations. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the validity of numerical results to ensure their accuracy and reliability. • Interpret the differences between various numerical methods for solving the same problem and choose the most appropriate one. • Compare Gaussian quadratures with other numerical integration methods. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply numerical methods to solve non-linear equations and systems of linear equations. • Use interpolation techniques to approximate function values. • Calculate integrals and derivatives numerically using appropriate methods. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Formulate real-world mathematical and engineering problems into numerically solvable problems. • Work efficiently within a team to discuss and apply numerical methods to complex problems. Communicate effectively about numerical methods and results with colleagues and specialists

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: mechanical extensors and their types, Kayla's theory, extensor fields, stress analysis, fracture and strain, current flow, fundamental laws of continuum mechanics, and applications to viscosity and fluidity
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify mechanical extensors. • Explain mechanical extensors and their types. • Recognize Kayla's theory.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Level • Defines mechanical extensors and their various types. • Explains the core principles of Kayla's theory. Cognitive Skills Level • Analyzes extensor fields and their effects. • Differentiates between fracture and strain in materials. Professional and Practical Skills Level • Applies fundamental laws of continuum mechanics to problem-solving. • Evaluates the applications of viscosity and fluidity in practical scenarios. General and Transferable Skills Level • Presents stress analysis results clearly. • Collaborates in discussing and interpreting current flow.

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: inverse functions, derivatives of inverse functions, derivatives of hyperbolic, inverse hyperbolic, and inverse trigonometric functions, and the relationship between inverse hyperbolic functions and the logarithmic function. It also covers various forms of L'Hôpital's Rule for limits. Integration methods include integration by substitution, by parts, and by partial fractions, along with applications of definite integrals. The course then moves to functions of several variables, partial derivatives, the chain rule, the equation of the tangent plane to a surface and its normal line, maxima and minima, and Taylor and Maclaurin expansions in two variables. Finally, it covers multiple integrals: double and triple integrals in Cartesian and polar coordinates, and triple integrals in Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify different functions and their derivatives. • Grasp various integration methods and partial derivatives. • Analyze the relationships between these concepts within a unified framework of knowledge
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify inverse functions, hyperbolic functions and their derivatives, and the different forms of L'Hôpital's Rule. • Explain various integration methods (by substitution, by parts, by partial fractions) and their applications to definite integrals. • Determine the concepts of functions of several variables, partial derivatives, and the chain rule. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the relationships between inverse hyperbolic functions and the logarithmic function. • Interpret the concept of the tangent plane and normal line, and the maximum and minimum values for multivariable functions. • Distinguish between different types of multiple integrals in Cartesian, polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply differentiation rules to inverse, hyperbolic, and inverse trigonometric functions. • Use multiple integration methods to calculate double and triple integrals in different coordinate systems. • Calculate Taylor and Maclaurin expansions for functions of two variables. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Formulate clear and organized solutions for complex mathematical problems in calculus. • Work efficiently within a team to discuss and clarify mathematical concepts with each other. • Communicate effectively about mathematical methods and results with colleagues and specialists

courses.courseDescription: This course delves into fluid statics, beginning with the main equation of fluid statics and exploring static forces on submerged planar and curved surfaces. It then transitions to fluid dynamics, introducing Lagrangian and Eulerian systems and analyzing particle derivatives and acceleration in both Cartesian and cylindrical coordinate systems. Key concepts like streamlines, pathlines, and streaklines are covered, leading into fundamental principles such as Bernoulli's theorem and the calculation of dynamic fluid pressure. Practical applications, including the Pitot tube and Venturi meter, are discussed alongside the essential continuity and motion equations. Further topics include vorticity and circulation, Stokes' flow equation, and the use of the complex potential function to understand phenomena like sources, sinks, and their duality. The course concludes with advanced concepts such as the circle theorem and Blasius' theorem
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify the properties of fluids (real and ideal fluids) and their potential energy. • Understand the fundamental forces resulting from fluid motion. • Classify flow in pipes and open channels and study energy loss during flow
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Level • Identifies fundamental concepts of number theory. • Explains relationships between different mathematical systems. Cognitive Skills Level • Analyzes complex problems using mathematical logic. • Compares various mathematical theories and models. Professional and Practical Skills Level • Applies mathematical tools and software to solve problems. • Designs innovative solutions for technical challenges. General and Transferable Skills Level • Communicates effectively about complex scientific ideas. • Collaborates within a team to complete research projects

courses.courseTitle: Software for Mathematical and Statistical Applications
courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: an introduction to symbolic computational software packages (e.g., Mathematica), an introduction to numerical computational software packages (e.g., MATLAB, SPSS), the use of computer programs in calculus and differential equations, and the application of numerical computation software to solve problems in numerical analysis.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Recognize symbolic computational software packages, such as Mathematica, and numerical computational software packages. • Understand how to use a computer program for calculus and differential equations
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Explain various symbolic and numerical computational software packages, such as Mathematica, MATLAB, and SPSS. • Determine how to use computer programs to solve problems related to calculus and differential equations. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze mathematical problems to identify the appropriate computational approach (symbolic or numerical) for solving them using software. • Interpret the results generated by computational software within the context of mathematical and scientific problems. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply computational software in calculus and solving differential equations. • Use numerical computation programs to solve practical problems in numerical analysis. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about statistical results. • Communicate effectively about the use of computational software and its results with colleagues and specialists. • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve complex problems that require the use of software tools

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: the concept of a ring and subring (their properties and examples), ring homomorphism and isomorphism, integral domains and fields, the field of quotients of an integral domain (the rational field of an integral domain), prime fields and the characteristic of a ring, polynomial rings (division and greatest common divisor), roots of polynomials over a field, ideals and quotient rings, direct sums of rings and their properties, ring spaces and Euclidean rings, field extensions (simple and finite extensions of fields), algebraic closure of a field, splitting fields, and finite fields.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify algebraic concepts and generalizations related to rings. • Deduce types of rings and operations on them.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Identify the concept of a ring, subring, and their properties. • Explain the relationships between homomorphism, ring isomorphism, and ideals. Cognitive Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Analyze the structure of integral domains, fields, and fields of quotients. • Distinguish between various types of field extensions, including simple and finite extensions. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Apply polynomial theories to calculate roots and the greatest common divisor. • Utilize concepts of prime fields and characteristics in constructing finite fields. General Transferable Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Manage time efficiently to complete tasks. • Work effectively in groups to solve complex problems

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Systems of Linear Equations and Matrices - Vectors in Two and Three Dimensions - General Vector Space - Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors - Matrix Diagonalization - Quadratic Form of Equations and Their Transformation to Canonical Form - Vector Spaces - Linear Independence - Dimensions and Basis Vectors of Spaces - Basis Transformation - Dot Product - Orthogonal Vectors - Linear Transformations, and their Applications
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Understand systems of linear equations, matrices, and vectors in two and three dimensions. • Grasp the quadratic form of equations and orthogonal vectors. • Explain the quadratic form of equations and how to convert them into canonical form, in addition to concepts of vector spaces, linear independence, dimensions, and basis vectors for spaces
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts of linear equation systems, matrices, vectors in two and three dimensions, and general vector spaces. • Explains the meaning of eigenvalues and eigenvectors and how to transform a matrix into its diagonal form. • Describes the quadratic form of an equation and its transformation into canonical form, in addition to concepts of vector spaces, linear independence, dimensions, and basis vectors of spaces. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes complex linear equation systems and identifies the best methods for solving them using matrices. • Infers the relationships between vectors in different spaces and applies concepts of linear independence and dimensions. • Applies linear transformations in various contexts and interprets their applications in different fields. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses specialized mathematical software to calculate eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and transform matrices. • Performs dot products and orthogonal vector operations accurately and uses them to solve geometric problems. • Develops strategies for solving complex problems related to vector spaces and their transformations. General and Transferable Skills • Collaborates effectively with colleagues in solving group problems and exchanging ideas about linear algebra concepts. • Communicates clearly and effectively about complex mathematical concepts, both in writing and orally. Thinks critically and systematically when facing mathematical challenges in linear algebra and its applications

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: metric spaces and fundamental inequalities. It covers open and closed sets, convergence, spherical neighborhoods, closure of a set and its properties, and complete metric spaces. The course then moves to normed spaces, subspaces of a normed space, and equivalent norms. Regarding linear operators on a normed space, it defines the linear, continuous, and bounded operator, linear operators on finite-dimensional spaces, and the inverse of a linear operator. Finally, it covers inner product spaces and Hilbert spaces, orthogonal sets, the Riesz Representation Theorem, properties of linear and bounded operators between Hilbert spaces, and adjoint, self-adjoint, normal, and unitary operators
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify metric spaces and normed spaces. • Determine the properties of linear operators in a normed space. • Explain Hilbert spaces and bounded operators in a Hilbert space
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify the fundamental concepts of metric spaces, normed spaces, complete spaces, and inner product spaces. • Explain the properties of linear operators (continuous, bounded, invertible) in normed spaces and Hilbert spaces. • Determine orthogonal sets in Hilbert spaces and adjoint, self-adjoint, normal, and unitary operators. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the relationships between open and closed sets and convergence in metric spaces. • Interpret Riesz Representation Theorem and the properties of bounded linear operators between two Hilbert spaces. • Distinguish between equivalent norms and their effect on the properties of normed spaces. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply fundamental inequalities in functional analysis to solve problems. • Use concepts of linear operators in finite-dimensional spaces to calculate the inverse of an operator. • Calculate the inner product of vectors to determine orthogonality in Hilbert spaces. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Work efficiently as part of a team to discuss and clarify abstract concepts. • Communicate effectively with colleagues and specialists in discussions.

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: wave-particle duality, wave packets, solving the Schrödinger equation for a free particle, solving the Schrödinger equation for a bound particle, quantum postulates, matrix mechanics, angular momentum, and spin.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify the fundamental principles and postulates of quantum mechanics. • Deduce the definition of the wave function and its statistical interpretation. • Understand the concept of operators and the uncertainty principle, and how to solve the Schrödinger equation and special functions for a physical system.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Identify wave-particle duality and the concept of wave packets. • Explain quantum postulates and matrix mechanics. Cognitive Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Analyze solutions to the Schrödinger equation for both free and bound particles. • Differentiate between the concepts of angular momentum and spin in quantum systems. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Apply quantum principles to understand particle behavior at atomic and subatomic levels. • Utilize mathematical models to calculate the quantum properties of physical systems. General Transferable Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Discuss clearly with peers the challenges and paradoxes encountered. • Work efficiently within a team to explore solutions for complex problems.

courses.courseDescription: This course covers fundamental concepts in statistics and probability, beginning with data organization, summarization, and presentation through tables, including relative and percentage frequency tables for both qualitative and quantitative data. It then delves into graphical representation for both types of data, followed by an exploration of measures of central tendency, percentiles, and dispersion. The course also introduces the principles of probability, covering concepts such as sets, statistical experiments, sample space, events, operations on events, mutually exclusive events, exhaustive events, and equally likely outcomes. Further topics include conditional probability, independent events, the definition of a random variable, selected discrete probability distributions, and the normal distribution, concluding with an introduction to correlation and regression
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: Understand, analyze, and apply statistical measures. Acquire knowledge and skills related to probability measures in quantitative and qualitative data across various fields
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify basic concepts in statistics and probability. • Explain the principles of probability. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze statistical data presented in tables and graphs, and derive meaningful information from them. • Interpret appropriate statistical methods and probability principles for processing and solving data-related problems. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply statistical techniques to collect, organize, and present actual data using appropriate tools. • Calculate various statistical measures such as measures of central tendency, dispersion, and basic probabilities. • Organize data for presentation in tables. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about statistical results. • Present interpretations and conclusions clearly and systematically. • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve problems. • Participate actively in discussions

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: electrostatic fields, their equations, and Gauss's Law in vacuum and dielectric materials; an introduction to conservative force fields, potential energy, and a study of electrostatic potential, Laplace's and Poisson's equations and their solutions; magnetic fields and their calculation, and Ampere's Law for magnetostatics; time-varying fields, Maxwell's equations, and the Law of Conservation of Charge; solving Maxwell's equations in vacuum, the propagation of electromagnetic waves in various media, magnetic power, the Poynting vector, and the electromagnetic wave spectrum
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Grasp the principle of field theory and its unification, starting with the simplest fields: electric and magnetic fields, and understand Maxwell's equations
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Level • Identifies the concepts of electrostatic fields and Gauss's Law. • Explains Maxwell's equations and the law of charge conservation. Cognitive Skills Level • Analyzes conservative force fields, potential energy, and electrostatic field potential. • Distinguishes between the propagation of electromagnetic waves in vacuum and various media. Professional and Practical Skills Level • Applies Laplace's and Poisson's equations to solve potential electrical problems. • Utilizes the Poynting vector to calculate magnetic power and electromagnetic wave energy. General Transferable Skills Level • Discusses complex scientific ideas clearly and effectively. • Collaborates effectively within a team to complete shared tasks

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Group Theory - Subgroups - Group Homomorphisms - Permutation Groups - Cyclic Groups - Group Isomorphism, and Quotient Groups - Geometric Transformation Groups - Rings, Ideals, and Quotient Rings - Subfields and Field Factorization - Algebraically Closed Fields - Integral Domains - Polynomials over a Field
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Acquire fundamental concepts in modern algebra, including groups, rings, and fields. • Differentiate between rings, ideals, and quotient rings, and grasp the concept of fields. • Deduce the properties of permutation groups, cyclic groups, and the isomorphism between groups and quotient groups.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts of Group Theory, Subgroups, and Homomorphisms between groups. • Explains the properties of Permutation Groups, Cyclic Groups, and the Isomorphism between groups and Quotient Groups. • Distinguishes between Rings, Ideals, and Quotient Rings, and understands the concept of Fields. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes problems related to groups and rings using appropriate mathematical theories and concepts. • Deduces new properties of algebraic structures based on given data and known theorems. • Applies abstract algebraic principles to solve complex mathematical problems concerning fields and integral domains. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses mathematical symbols and terminology accurately and effectively in scientific communication regarding abstract algebra. • Executes complex algebraic operations on groups, rings, and fields efficiently. • Identifies logical errors in proofs or mathematical solutions presented within an algebraic context. General and Transferable Skills • Collaborates effectively in solving group problems and exchanging mathematical ideas. • Communicates clearly and effectively about complex mathematical concepts, both in writing and orally. • Thinks critically and systematically when facing new mathematical challenges.

courses.courseDescription: This course's content includes: the concept of a function, its properties, operations on functions, types of functions, function composition, and inverse functions. It covers the concept of limits, properties of limits, the concept of a function's limit at infinity, and the concept of right-hand and left-hand limits, along with methods for calculating limits. The course also delves into the concept of continuity, its properties, and theorems on continuity. Furthermore, it examines the concept of differentiation, the relationship between differentiation and continuity, differentiation rules, trigonometric functions, derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions, hyperbolic functions, derivatives of inverse hyperbolic functions, derivatives of exponential and logarithmic functions, higher-order derivatives and Leibniz's Theorem, the chain rule, implicit differentiation, and parametric forms of functions, along with a study of some applications of differentiation. Finally, the course covers integration: integration of algebraic functions, integration of exponential and logarithmic functions, integration of trigonometric and inverse trigonometric functions, and integration of hyperbolic and inverse hyperbolic functions
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify the concepts of functions and limits. • Grasp the concepts of continuity and differentiation, and determine their properties and relationships.
courses.courseOutcomes: knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define the concept of a function, its properties, types, and operations, including function composition and inverse functions. • Explain the concept of limits, their properties, methods of calculation, limits at infinity, and right-hand and left-hand limits. • Identify the concept of continuity, its properties, and related theorems. • Describe the concept of differentiation, its relationship with continuity, and the rules of differentiation for various functions. • Summarize the types of integrals for algebraic, trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, and logarithmic functions. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the behavior of functions as they approach specific points or infinity to determine their limits. • Interpret the relationship between higher-order derivatives and Leibniz's Theorem. • Distinguish between methods for differentiating implicit functions and parametric forms of functions. • Infer applications of differentiation in solving various mathematical problems. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply differentiation rules to trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, logarithmic, and inverse functions. • Use the chain rule and differentiation of implicit and parametric functions to calculate derivatives. • Calculate definite and indefinite integrals for algebraic, trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, and logarithmic functions. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Formulate clear and organized solutions for mathematical problems in calculus. • Work efficiently as part of a team to discuss and clarify complex mathematical concepts. • Communicate effectively about mathematical methods and results with colleagues and supervisors

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Review of Simple Harmonic Motion - Damped Harmonic Motion - Examples and Applications of Damped Harmonic Motion - Central Orbits - Applications of Central Orbits - Kepler's Laws - Introduction to Space Dynamics - Circular Coordinate Systems - Motion Near the Earth's Surface and Foucault's Pendulum - Velocity and Acceleration in Circular Systems in Cylindrical Coordinates - Velocity and Acceleration in Circular Systems in Polar and Spherical Coordinates.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Apply scientific facts and theories of particle dynamics. • Identify different patterns in particle dynamics
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines advanced concepts of simple and damped harmonic motion and their applications. • Explains the principles of central orbits and Kepler's Laws in dynamics. • Describes the fundamentals of space dynamics and how to calculate velocity and acceleration in cylindrical, polar, and spherical coordinates. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes complex problems related to damped harmonic motion and its applications in physical systems. • Infers kinematic relationships for objects in central orbits based on Kepler's Laws. • Applies laws of motion in space to calculate velocity and acceleration in various coordinate systems. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses appropriate mathematical equations to describe motion near the Earth's surface and determine the behavior of Foucault's pendulum. • Executes precise calculations for velocity and acceleration in cylindrical, polar, and spherical coordinates. • Develops problem-solving skills related to advanced dynamics and complex physical systems. General and Transferable Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about statistical results. • Present interpretations and conclusions clearly and organized. • Work efficiently within a team to solve problems. • Participate effectively in discussions.

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: spatial statics, friction force and normal reaction, slipping and overturning, center of gravity, virtual work, stability of equilibrium, and reduction of force systems.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Recognize the fundamental principles in statics. • Grasp information related to vector algebra, the weight of bodies and surfaces, and types of equilibrium.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define fundamental concepts of spatial statics, friction force, and center of gravity. • Explain the principles of slipping, overturning, and equilibrium stability in statistical systems. Intellectual Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the effect of friction force and normal reaction on the movement and equilibrium of bodies. • Interpret the principles of virtual work and the reduction of force systems within the context of statics. Professional and Practical Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply the laws of spatial statics to calculate forces and torques in three dimensions. • Calculate friction coefficients and use them in analyzing the equilibrium of bodies prone to slipping or overturning. Transferable Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about statistical results. • Present interpretations and conclusions clearly and systematically. • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve problems. • Participate actively in discussions.

courses.courseTitle: Introduction to Number Theory and logic
courses.courseDescription: This course covers: numerical identities – linear congruence and the theory of residues – primitive roots and indices – quadratic residues, Legendre symbol, and the law of quadratic reciprocity – arithmetic functions – basic Diophantine equations – infinite continued fractions and rational approximations of real numbers – Pell’s equation – distribution of prime numbers
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be aware of the fundamental concepts of number theory, recognize key ideas in prime number theory and their relationship to algebraic number theory, appreciate the importance of number theory, and develop mathematical proof skills
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:Identify the fundamental concepts of number theory, Understand arithmetic functions. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to: Analyze the distribution of prime numbers. , Apply the law of quadratic reciprocity. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to: Apply prime number theory. , Solve basic Diophantine equations. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to: Organize and complete required tasks , Use arithmetic skills in everyday life.

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: Coulomb’s law, Gauss’s theorem, electric field and lines of force, equipotential surface, electric dipole, Poisson’s and Laplace’s equations, Poisson transformations, solving Laplace equations, and the continuity equation.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to understand the fundamental concepts and theories in the fields of electricity, magnetism, and alternating current.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:State the fundamental theories in the field of electricity, Identify the basic concepts of magnetism. B) Cognitive Skills: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: Differentiate between electric field intensity and lines of force. C) Practical and Professional Skills: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: Apply Gauss’s theorem in relevant situations. D) Key Transferable Skills: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: Use analytical skills, Solve related problems

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: an introduction to Graph Theory, applications of the theory, vector forms/shapes, basic concepts and theories about forms/shapes, algorithms, shape theory, and computer programs.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify the concepts of Graph Theory. • Deduce the concepts associated with Graph Theory. • Determine the uses of Graph Theory in studying mathematical graphs.
