courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: an introduction to planetary mechanics and its applications, the motion of artificial satellites and spacecraft in space, orbital elements, converting orbital elements into position and velocity vectors, types of space orbits, and space orbit design.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Understand planetary mechanics. • Grasp the applications of planetary mechanics, the motion of artificial satellites, and spacecraft in space.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Level • Identifies fundamental concepts of planetary mechanics and their applications. • Explains the motion of artificial satellites and spacecraft in space. Cognitive Skills Level • Analyzes orbital elements and their conversion into position and velocity vectors. • Distinguishes between different types of space orbits. Professional and Practical Skills Level • Applies engineering principles in the design of space orbits. • Utilizes acquired knowledge to simulate the motion of celestial bodies. General and Transferable Skills Level • Communicates clearly about complex aspects of planetary mechanics. • Collaborates within a team to explore space navigation challenges.

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: the concept of topology, definitions of topological spaces, closed and open sets, interior and boundary regions, first and second countability axioms, separable spaces, methods of generating topology on sets, interior and closure operators, bases and sub-bases, subspaces, Cartesian products, sums, embedding, local embedding, and metrizable topological spaces.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify the concept of topology, topological spaces, Cartesian products, and metrizable topological spaces. • Grasp interpretations of topology and various topological spaces, as well as open and closed sets. • Infer interior and closure operators, bases and sub-bases, and the concepts of local embedding and metrizable spaces.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify the concept of topology and various topological spaces, as well as open and closed sets. • Explain the first and second countability axioms, separable spaces, and methods for generating topology on sets. • Determine interior and closure operators, bases and sub-bases, and the concepts of local embedding and metrizable spaces. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the properties of spherical neighborhoods and the closure of sets in topological spaces. • Interpret the relationship between Cartesian products, sums, and embedding within the context of topological spaces. • Distinguish between different types of topological spaces based on their properties (e.g., complete and metrizable spaces). Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply topological concepts to determine the interior and boundary regions of a given set. • Use rules for generating topology to construct new topologies on given sets. • Calculate convergence properties in various topological spaces.

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: vectors in space, various forms of the equation of a straight line in space, the vector and parametric equations of a space curve, the relationship between two straight lines in space (parallelism, intersection, skew lines), the equation of a plane in space, the equation of a family of planes, the relationship between a straight line and a plane, the intersection of two planes in space, equations of surfaces of revolution in space (solids of conic surfaces, the sphere, the cone), and the intersection of planes with space surfaces
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify vectors in space and the different forms of the equation of a straight line in space. • Understand the vector and parametric equations of a space curve. • Deduce the relationship between two straight lines in space
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Identify the concept of vectors in space and the different forms of equations for straight lines and planes. • Explain the relationship between straight lines and planes in space. Cognitive Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Analyze the geometric relationships between lines, planes, and surfaces of revolution in space. • Differentiate between the various types of intersections of planes with space surfaces. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Apply vector and parametric equations to describe curves and space surfaces. • Utilize concepts of spatial geometry to solve engineering and scientific problems. General Transferable Skills After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to: • Discuss complex mathematical ideas and concepts clearly with colleagues. • Work effectively within a team to analyze and solve engineering problems.

courses.courseDescription: The course includes the following topics: solving second-order differential equations, Bessel and Legendre equations, Laplace transform method, systems of equations, existence and uniqueness theorems for first- and second-order differential equations, finite difference equations, and first-order partial differential equations.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to understand first-order and first-degree differential equations, various types of linear differential equations, and distinguish between the fundamental theories of ordinary differential equations.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:Identify the order of differential equations,Recognize the existence and uniqueness theorem. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Distinguish between linear differential equations,Compare the fundamental theories of ordinary differential equations. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Solve linear differential equations.,Solve first- and second-order differential equations. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Manage time effectively,Apply scientific thinking.

courses.courseDescription: The course covers the following topics: the concept of system and surroundings, types of systems, types of processes in thermodynamics (isothermal and adiabatic processes), extensive and intensive properties, the concept of free energy, enthalpy, and entropy, the zeroth law of thermodynamics and the reason behind its name, the first law of thermodynamics, work, the relationship between CVC_VCV and CPC_PCP, Hess's law, entropy as a state function, laws of chemical kinetics, rate laws, calculation of reaction rates and rate constants, rate expressions, stoichiometric measurements, reaction order, concentration profiles for reactions, integrated rate equations for simple reactions, quantitative studies of half-life times for different reactions, pseudo-order reactions, zero-order reactions, and general order reactions
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to identify various thermodynamic laws that explain chemical kinetics using data analysis methods, equations, and theoretical frameworks.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:Define the concept of a system and its surroundings ,Identify extensive and intensive properties., Explain the concepts of free energy, enthalpy, and entropy. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Analyze the laws of chemical kinetics.,Use rate laws and calculate reaction rates and rate constants. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Analyze the concentration profile of reactions.,Apply integrated rate equations for simple reactions. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to :Evaluate information .,Manage time and set priorities ,Meet deadlines

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Cartesian, Cylindrical, and Spherical Coordinates - Functions of Two Variables - Functions of Three Variables - Limits - Continuity - Partial Derivatives - Chain Rule - Extreme Values of Functions of Two Variables - Lagrange Multipliers - Double Integrals and their Applications - Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates - Triple Integrals and their Applications - Triple Integrals in Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates - Sequences - Infinite Series - Convergence Tests - Representation of Functions by Power Series - Taylor and Maclaurin Series, and Binomial Series.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Generalize single-variable function concepts to multivariable functions. • Identify various applications of functions. • Describe the concept of extreme values and functions of two variables using Lagrange multipliers, along with different types of multiple integrals (double and triple) in various coordinate systems
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts of Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical coordinate systems, as well as functions of two and three variables. • Explains the concepts of limits, continuity, partial derivatives, and the chain rule in the context of multivariable functions. • Describes the concept of extreme values and functions of two variables using Lagrange multipliers, in addition to various types of multiple integrals (double and triple) in different coordinate systems. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes the behavior of multivariable functions at critical points and determines their extreme values. • Infers the convergence or divergence of sequences and infinite series using various convergence tests. • Applies double and triple integrals to solve geometric and physical problems, and utilizes them in polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses series (such as power series, Taylor, and Maclaurin series) to represent and approximate functions. • Executes complex partial differentiation operations and multiple integrals with accuracy. • Develops strategies for solving problems involving coordinate transformations and the calculation of Lagrange multipliers. General and Transferable Skills • Collaborates effectively in solving complex problems related to multivariable calculus. • Communicates clearly and effectively about mathematical concepts and theories in calculus, both in writing and orally. • Thinks critically and systematically when dealing with new mathematical challenges in this field.

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Basic Concepts in Analytical Dynamics - Lagrange's Equations for Holonomic Dynamical Systems - Derivation of Lagrange's Equations and Definition of the Lagrangian Function - Atwood Machine and Real-Life Applications - Hamilton's Function and Derivation of Hamilton's Equations - Jacobi Integrals and Hamilton's Principle - Derivation of Hamilton's Equations using Hamilton's Principle - Poisson Brackets - Proof of Jacobi-Poisson Theorem - Equilibrium Position
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Identify theories and laws in analytical dynamics. • Derive methods for data analysis, equations, and theories. • Recognize real-life applications of analytical dynamics.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the fundamental concepts in analytical dynamics and the theory of Lagrange's equations. • Explains the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian functions and how to derive Hamilton's equations. • Describes Jacobi integrals and Hamilton's principle, as well as Poisson brackets and the Jacobi-Poisson theorem. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes holonomic dynamical systems and applies Lagrange's and Hamilton's equations to them. • Infers the equilibrium position of complex dynamical systems using analytical principles. • Applies theoretical concepts in analytical dynamics to solve real-life application examples. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses mathematical principles to derive equations of motion for physical systems. • Executes equation derivations and calculates Poisson brackets with accuracy. • Develops mathematical proof skills to demonstrate theorems such as the Jacobi-Poisson theorem. General and Transferable Skills • Communicates effectively about statistical results. • Presents interpretations and conclusions clearly and in an organized manner. • Works efficiently within a team to solve problems. • Participates effectively in discussions.

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem. It covers point estimation and the properties of estimators (unbiasedness, mean squared error, consistency, sufficiency, minimal sufficiency). The course also delves into the exponential family, the Cramér-Rao inequality, Fisher information, the Rao-Blackwell Theorem (sufficiency and completeness), and the Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem. Estimation methods covered include the method of moments and maximum likelihood estimators with their asymptotic properties. It also explores the use of prior density functions, invariance methods, interval estimation, confidence interval estimators, pivotal methods, and Bayesian credible intervals.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify important statistical methods and concepts related to hypothesis testing, parameter estimation, and confidence intervals for these parameters. • Recognize theories and properties associated with probability theory
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify fundamental concepts in mathematical statistics, such as sampling distributions, properties of estimators, and the Central Limit Theorem. • Explain the relationship between the Cramér-Rao inequality and Fisher information, as well as the Rao-Blackwell and Lehmann-Scheffé theorems. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the properties of different estimators (unbiasedness, consistency, sufficiency) to assess their efficiency. • Interpret results derived from point and interval estimation methods, and confidence intervals for population parameters. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply various estimation methods, such as the method of moments and maximum likelihood estimators, to calculate parameter estimates. • Calculate confidence intervals for population parameters using pivotal methods and Bayesian credible intervals. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Communicate effectively about statistical results. • Formulate logical arguments regarding the selection of the most appropriate statistical estimators for a given situation. • Work within a team to discuss challenges in statistical estimation and develop solutions for them

courses.courseDescription: This course's scientific content includes: the concept of inferential statistics; sampling theory, its importance and applications in society; the normal distribution and standard normal distribution, along with the table of critical values for the standard normal distribution. It also covers the chi-square distribution, theories explaining its relationship to the normal distribution, applied examples, and its critical values table. The course introduces the t-distribution, theories explaining its relationship to the normal distribution, applied examples, and its values table. Additionally, it examines the F-distribution, theories explaining its relationship to the normal distribution, applied examples, and its values table. Key topics also include the definition, importance, and practical applications of hypothesis testing, specifically chi-square, t-tests, and F-tests. Finally, the course defines simple and complex analysis of variance and simple linear regression.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify concepts and principles related to inferential statistics. • Grasp the principles of inferential statistics and their real-life applications
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define the concept of inferential statistics and the importance of sampling theory and its applications. • Explain the differences between the normal distribution, standard normal distribution, and the chi-square, t, and F distributions. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the relationship between different statistical distributions (such as the normal distribution and chi-square, t, F). • Interpret the results of statistical hypothesis tests and simple and complex analysis of variance. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply statistical hypothesis tests (such as chi-square, t, F tests) to various data sets. • Calculate simple linear regression coefficients and use them for prediction. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Present interpretations and conclusions systematically. • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve problems

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: complex numbers, polar representation, complex functions, limits, continuity, analytic functions, elementary complex functions (trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, logarithmic, and complex power functions), differentiation, definite integrals, complex line integrals, infinite series, Taylor series, Laurent series, Residue Theorem, applications in real and improper integrals, and physical and engineering applications, as well as Cauchy's Integral Theorem.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Recognize the importance of using numerical methods to solve a variety of scientific problems. • Explain interpolation methods, numerical integration and differentiation, and matrix analysis methods. • Identify the fundamental principles for solving systems of linear equations and ordinary differential equations. • Apply numerical methods to solve various scientific problems, finding approximate solutions to the problems presented in different fields
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Define complex numbers and their various representations, including polar representation. • Explain the concepts of limits, continuity, and analytic functions in complex analysis. • Identify elementary complex functions such as trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential, logarithmic, and complex power functions. • Describe Cauchy's Residue and Integral Theorems, and the concepts of infinite series, Taylor series, and Laurent series. Intellectual Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze the properties of complex functions to determine their differentiability and analyticity. • Interpret the relationship between complex analysis and its applications in real and improper integrals. • Distinguish between different types of infinite series in the complex plane and their convergence properties. Professional and Practical Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply differentiation and integration rules to complex functions. • Use the Residue Theorem to calculate complex line integrals and complex real integrals. • Compute Taylor and Laurent series expansions for complex functions around specific points. Transferable Skills After studying this course, students are expected to be able to: • Formulate mathematical and engineering problems that require the use of complex analysis. • Work efficiently within a team to discuss and clarify complex concepts in complex analysis. Communicate effectively about mathematical methods and results with colleagues and specialists

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: linear programming (graphical and algebraic methods, the simplex method, dual simplex method, and parametric analysis), error analysis, transportation problems and the transportation model, and integer programming (cutting plane method, linear analysis, branch and bound method). It also covers dynamic programming and various solution methods using dynamic programming.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Identify concepts related to the science of operations research, such as linear programming. • Grasp linear analysis, dynamic programming, and solution methods using dynamic programming.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Identify fundamental concepts in operations research, such as linear programming, parametric analysis, and integer programming. • Explain various solution methods in linear programming (graphical, algebraic, and simplex methods) and dynamic programming. Intellectual Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Analyze linear programming problems using the simplex method, dual simplex method, and parametric analysis. • Interpret the results of linear and dynamic analysis to derive optimal decisions. Professional and Practical Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Apply graphical, algebraic, and simplex methods to solve linear programming and transportation problems. • Calculate solutions for dynamic programming and integer programming problems using appropriate methods. Transferable Skills After completing this course, students are expected to be able to: • Formulate real-world problems into mathematical models solvable using operations research. • Work efficiently as part of a team to solve complex problems requiring mathematical models and quantitative analysis.

courses.courseDescription: The course's scientific content includes: Biomathematics: Concept and Importance - Mathematical Modeling - Dynamical Systems as Differential Equations - Optimal Formulas for Solutions of Dynamical Differential Equations - Growth Equations - Competition for Fixed Resources - Applications of Exponential Functions in Biology - Time-Concentration Curves in Blood Injected with Drugs via Separation - Common Growth Functions - Exponential Curves - Time Period for Retaining Carbon Dioxide in the Lungs During Respiration - Measurement of Cardiac Output - Communication Science and Insufficiency - Differential Equations for Epidemics - Bacteriology - Mechanism of Reproduction and Extinction - Membrane Diffusion
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, you'll be able to: • Understand differential equations and mathematical modeling for comprehending biological systems. • Describe how to measure cardiac output, the mechanisms of bacterial reproduction and extinction, and the concept of membrane diffusion. • Explain the growth function and the applications of exponential functions in biology.
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding • Defines the concept and importance of biomathematics, along with the principles of mathematical modeling for dynamical systems as differential equations. • Explains the growth function, the concept of competition for fixed resources, and the applications of exponential functions in biology. • Describes how to measure cardiac output, the mechanisms of bacterial reproduction and extinction, and the concept of membrane diffusion. Intellectual Skills • Analyzes time-concentration curves in drug-injected blood to extract biological information. • Infers optimal formulas for solutions of dynamical differential equations applied in biological systems. • Applies differential equations to model epidemics and understand their dynamics. Professional and Practical Skills • Uses common functions (like exponential functions) to represent growth and decay phenomena in biology. • Executes calculations related to the time period for retaining carbon dioxide in the lungs during respiration. • Develops simple mathematical models to describe bacterial reproduction and extinction mechanisms, and membrane diffusion. General and Transferable Skills • Communicates effectively about statistical results. • Presents interpretations and conclusions clearly and in an organized manner. • Works efficiently within a team to solve problems. • Participates effectively in discussions

courses.courseDescription: The scientific content of this course includes: periodic functions – binary functions – monotonic functions – limits – chain rule – mean value theorem – Leibniz’s theorem – Taylor series – Maclaurin series – homogeneous functions – Euler’s theorem for homogeneous functions – improper integrals – sets – subsets – cyclic groups – groups – Lagrange’s theorem – group symmetries – vectors – scalar product – rigid body – moments – couples – equilibrium – center of gravity – vector operators (gradient of a scalar function, divergence of a vector field, curl of a vector) – Stokes' theorem – velocity – acceleration – relative velocity – impulse – driving force – polar coordinates – simple harmonic motion – sample space – events – probability – permutations – combinations – conditional probability
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to explain concepts, facts, and principles in pure and applied mathematics, and statistics, and identify related theories and laws in English.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After studying this course, each student is expected to be able to:Name the different types of functions in English,State the various function-related theorems in English. B) Cognitive Skills: After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to:Differentiate between the principles of pure and applied mathematics in English.,Interpret the various functions in English. C) Practical and Professional Skills: After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to:Apply the principles of pure and applied mathematics ,Utilize various theorems in teaching mathematics in English. D) Key Transferable Skills: After studying this course, the student is expected to be able to:Motivate themselves to seek out information and expand their mathematical knowledge in English beyond the course content.

courses.courseDescription: The course covers physical and mechanical problems and integral equations, linear integral equations, classification and solutions of differential and integral equations, Fredholm integral equations of the first and second kind, Volterra integral equations of the first and second kind, characteristic behavior of integral equations, and applications to ordinary differential equations.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to understand various methods for solving Fredholm and Volterra integral equations.
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:Classify differential and integral equations,Identify the characteristic behavior of integral equations. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Distinguish between first- and second-kind Volterra integral equations. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Apply integral equations to ordinary differential equations,Solve integral equations. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Analyze data, Demonstrate new skills.

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: Local Curve Theory: curvature, torsion, Serret-Frenet formulas (or Frenet-Serret theory), existence and uniqueness theorem for curves. Plane Curves: non-isometric, four-vertex theorem, rotation. Local Surface Theory: first fundamental form, normal and geodesic curvature, parallelism, second fundamental form, Weingarten maps, types of curvature, and constant curvature surfaces.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Understand the local theory of curves • Analyze planar curves and identify the four-vertex theorem • Describe surface theory and fundamental forms
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the local theory of surfaces • Summarize the existence and uniqueness theorem of curves B) Intellectual Skills: Students will be able to: • Classify Weingarten maps • Distinguish between normal and geodesic curvature C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students will be able to: • Apply the local theory of curves • Analyze different types of curvature D) Transferable Skills: Students will be able to: • Analyze data • Collaborate effectively with peers • Use scientific research skills

courses.courseDescription: The course content includes: Introduction to Special Relativity, postulates of Special Relativity and Lorentz transformations, relativistic kinematics, geometrical representation of Special Relativity and Minkowski space, relativistic mechanics, Einstein's energy equation and various results, applications of Special Relativity (mechanical applications, applications in modern physics, and applications in chemistry)
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to: • Identify the scientific facts and concepts of the Theory of Relativity. • Deduce examples of applications of the Theory of Relativity
courses.courseOutcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Level • Identifies the postulates of Special Relativity and Lorentz transformations. • Explains the concept of Minkowski space and the geometrical representation of Special Relativity. Cognitive Skills Level • Analyzes relativistic kinematics and mechanics. • Distinguishes between the different applications of Special Relativity in physics and chemistry. Professional and Practical Skills Level • Applies Einstein's energy equation to solve physical problems. • Utilizes the principles of Relativity Theory in interpreting modern phenomena. General Transferable Skills Level • Communicates clearly and effectively with others. • Collaborates effectively within a team to accomplish shared tasks

courses.courseDescription: The course includes the following topics: fundamental concepts, stress theory, equilibrium equations, principal stress surfaces, stress theory, stress conditions, fundamental stress components, strain energy, the relationship between stress and strain components (Hooke’s Law), fundamental problems in elasticity, Lame’s equations, Beltrami’s equations, plane stress, and plane strain.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of this course, the student will be able to identify the scientific facts and theories of elasticity, effectively apply information technology related to elasticity theory, and select appropriate solutions for basic and specific equations of elasticity theory
courses.courseOutcomes: A) Knowledge and Understanding: After completing this course, students are expected to be able to:Define stress and strain theory,State the conditions of stress. B) Intellectual Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Analyze stress conditions and fundamental stress components, Compare scientific theories of elasticity. C) Professional and Practical Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Apply elasticity theory, Solve fundamental problems in elasticity. D) Transferable and Generic Skills: Students are expected to be able to:Use information technology, Develop innovative solutions.

courses.courseTitle: Information and Communication Technologies in Education and Research
courses.courseDescription: The course covers the principles of computer science, concepts of e-learning, and interaction with the university's educational platforms such as Learning Management Systems (LMS) and Student Information Systems (SIS). It aims to enhance students' skills and abilities to communicate effectively online and complete academic assignments. The course also includes concepts of artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and cybersecurity, as well as the use of the internet in education and scientific research.
courses.courseObjectives: By the end of the course, students will be able to: • Acquire foundational knowledge in Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and its applications in the field of education. • Develop study skills and enhance knowledge of fundamental computer systems applications and big data.
courses.courseOutcomes: A. Knowledge & Understanding At the end of the module, each student will be expected to: - Explain the principles of computer science. - Clarify e-learning concepts. B. Cognitive Skills At the end of the module, each student will be expected to: - Engage with the university’s educational platforms. - Distinguish between the concepts of artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and cybersecurity. C. Practical and Professional Skills At the end of the module, each student will be expected to: - Utilize the internet in educational contexts. - Use information technology in scientific research. D. Key Transferable Skills At the end of the module, each student will be expected to: - Develop scientific research skills.
